note: There was no single front: armies crossed a whole continent, by plains, mountains and sea. The areas show roughly who held the ground; they are approximate, especially where guerrilla bands and small garrisons changed hands often.

chapters.title: The juntas of 1810 and the First Republic
chapters.text: With Spain's king a prisoner of Napoleon, Caracas deposed its captain general on 19 April 1810 and set up a junta, and on 5 July 1811 seven of Venezuela's ten provinces declared independence. Coro, Maracaibo and Guayana stayed loyal to Spain. In March 1812 a small royalist force under Domingo de Monteverde marched out of Coro, an earthquake wrecked the republican towns, and people flocked to the royalists. Valencia fell in May, Bolívar lost the fortress of Puerto Cabello, and on 25 July Francisco de Miranda surrendered at San Mateo.

chapters.title: From Cartagena to Caracas: the Admirable Campaign
chapters.text: In exile in Cartagena, Bolívar blamed the fall of the republic on weak, divided government in his Cartagena Manifesto of December 1812. Fighting for New Granada, he cleared the royalists from the Magdalena River and took Cúcuta, then crossed into Venezuela in May 1813. At Trujillo he declared 'war to the death' on Spaniards who did not join him, while Santiago Mariño freed the east. Bolívar entered Caracas on 6 August 1813.

chapters.title: War to the death: the fall of the Second Republic
chapters.text: The restored republic did not win over the poor. On the plains, the royalist José Tomás Boves raised an army of llaneros, cowboys of every colour, who fought with the same no-quarter savagery as the republicans. After victories at Araure, La Victoria and San Mateo, the republic was crushed at La Puerta on 15 June 1814; Boves took Caracas in July and thousands fled east. Boves was killed winning at Urica in December, and the last republicans fell at Maturín.

chapters.title: Chile lost and won: Rancagua to Maipú
arrows: San Martín and O'Higgins cross by the Los Patos pass (January–February 1817)
Las Heras crosses by the Uspallata pass (January–February 1817)
chapters.text: In the south the other front opened. A royalist army from Peru destroyed Chile's patriots at Rancagua in October 1814, and Bernardo O'Higgins fled to Mendoza, where José de San Martín was building the Army of the Andes. In January 1817 San Martín led about 4,000 men over passes some 3,000 metres high, won at Chacabuco on 12 February and entered Santiago. A new royalist army surprised him at Cancha Rayada in March 1818, but his victory at Maipú on 5 April made Chile's independence secure.

chapters.title: Morillo's reconquest and the Jamaica Letter
arrows: Morillo's army sails to Santa Marta (July 1815)
Calzada invades from the Venezuelan plains (October 1815 – May 1816)
chapters.text: With Napoleon beaten, Ferdinand VII sent Pablo Morillo with about 10,000 men, the largest army Spain had ever sent to America. Morillo landed in Venezuela in April 1815, then besieged Cartagena, which starved for 105 days before it fell on 6 December. While New Granada's divided republicans retreated, Bolívar, exiled in Jamaica, wrote his Jamaica Letter, a vision of free Spanish American nations. Royalist columns took Bogotá on 6 May 1816 and executed many of the republic's leaders.

chapters.title: Angostura and the plains
arrows: Bolívar advances from the Apure towards Caracas (February–March 1818)
chapters.text: Back from Haiti, where President Alexandre Pétion armed him in return for a promise to free the slaves, Bolívar made his base on the Orinoco. Manuel Piar beat the royalists at San Félix, and Angostura fell on 17 July 1817, giving the patriots a river port open to the world. José Antonio Páez and his plainsmen held the Apure, but Bolívar's march on Caracas failed in 1818. In February 1819 he opened the Congress of Angostura, which elected him president.

chapters.title: Over the Andes to Boyacá
arrows: Over the Andes by the Páramo de Pisba (June–July 1819)
Boyacá and the road to Bogotá (7–10 August 1819)
chapters.text: In the rainy season, when no one expected an army to move, Bolívar marched west across the flooded plains, joined Francisco de Paula Santander at Tame and climbed the freezing Páramo de Pisba, losing many men and nearly all his horses. Descending into New Granada in July, he fought the royalists at Vargas Swamp and slipped past them to Tunja. At Boyacá on 7 August 1819 he trapped José María Barreiro's army, and three days later he entered Bogotá, which the viceroy had abandoned.

chapters.title: Gran Colombia and Carabobo
arrows: Bolívar's army marches from New Granada (April–June 1821)
Carabobo and the march to Caracas (24–29 June 1821)
chapters.text: On 17 December 1819 the Congress at Angostura joined Venezuela and New Granada into one Republic of Colombia, later called Gran Colombia. A revolution in Spain in 1820 cut off Morillo's reinforcements, and he agreed a truce with Bolívar. When Maracaibo went over to the republic in January 1821 the war resumed, and on 24 June Bolívar and Páez routed the royalists at Carabobo. Bolívar entered Caracas on 29 June; only a few fortresses such as Puerto Cabello held out.

chapters.title: San Martín lands in Peru
arrows: The Liberating Expedition sails from Valparaíso (August–September 1820)
Arenales's march through the highlands (October 1820 – January 1821)
The army moves north by sea (October–November 1820)
chapters.text: Peru was the heart of royal power, so San Martín carried the war there by sea. His Liberating Expedition of about 4,000 men, mostly Chileans, landed at Paracas in September 1820, while Lord Cochrane's fleet swept the coast and Juan Antonio Álvarez de Arenales marched through the highlands. Trujillo and the north declared for independence, and in July 1821 the viceroy abandoned Lima. San Martín proclaimed Peru's independence on 28 July, and the fortress of Callao surrendered in September.

chapters.title: Pichincha and the Guayaquil meeting
arrows: Sucre's march by Cuenca to Quito (January–May 1822)
chapters.text: The port of Guayaquil threw off Spanish rule on 9 October 1820, and Bolívar sent Antonio José de Sucre to take Quito. After two failed attempts, Sucre marched south round the mountains by Cuenca and north up the Andes, while Bolívar fought a costly battle at Bomboná near Pasto. On 24 May 1822 Sucre won on the slopes of the Pichincha volcano and Quito surrendered. In July Bolívar and San Martín met at Guayaquil; San Martín soon left Peru, and the war there passed to Bolívar.

chapters.title: Junín and Ayacucho
arrows: The royalists fall back towards Cuzco (August–September 1824)
La Serna's army marches on Sucre (October–December 1824)
chapters.text: The royalists still held the Peruvian highlands, and they twice took Lima, in June 1823 and again in February 1824, after the garrison of Callao mutinied and handed the fortress to Spain. Named dictator of Peru, Bolívar gathered his army in the north and marched south over the Andes. His cavalry won at Junín on 6 August 1824, fought with lances and sabres. On 9 December Sucre beat the viceroy's larger army at Ayacucho, and the viceroy and his generals surrendered.

chapters.title: Bolivia and the last stronghold
chapters.text: One royalist general, Pedro Antonio de Olañeta, refused to give up Upper Peru. Sucre marched in from February 1825 as royalist units changed sides, and Olañeta was mortally wounded at Tumusla on 1 April. On 6 August 1825 an assembly at Chuquisaca declared Upper Peru independent and named it after Bolívar. In the fortress of Callao, José Ramón Rodil held out through a year of siege and hunger until he surrendered on 23 January 1826, the end of Spanish rule in South America.

battles.name: Battle of Cúcuta
battles.casualties: About 16 patriots and 60 royalists killed or wounded

battles.name: Battle of Araure
battles.casualties: About 1,800 dead: some 800 patriots and 1,000 royalists

battles.name: Battle of San Mateo
battles.casualties: Estimates vary widely: perhaps 1,000–3,000 killed or wounded on both sides

battles.name: First Battle of Carabobo
battles.casualties: About 50 republicans and 2,100–3,000 royalists

battles.name: Second Battle of La Puerta
battles.casualties: About 1,000 republicans killed and 1,500 prisoners put to death; some 200 royalists killed

battles.name: Battle of Urica
battles.casualties: Perhaps 1,600–2,500 dead on both sides, Boves among them

battles.name: Battle of Rancagua
battles.casualties: About 240 royalists and 700 patriots killed or wounded; 600 patriots captured

battles.name: Battle of Chacabuco
battles.casualties: About 100 patriots and 500 royalists killed or wounded; 600 royalists captured

battles.name: Battle of Cancha Rayada
battles.casualties: About 450 patriots killed or wounded and some 2,000 scattered

battles.name: Battle of Maipú
battles.casualties: About 1,000 patriots and 2,000 royalists killed; some 3,000 royalists captured

battles.name: Siege of Cartagena
battles.casualties: Defenders: about 200 killed and 400 prisoners executed; besiegers: about 3,000 dead, most of disease

battles.name: Battle of San Félix
battles.casualties: About 100 republicans killed or wounded; about 600 royalists killed and 500 captured

battles.name: Battle of Matasiete
battles.casualties: About 560 royalists killed or wounded; republican losses unknown

battles.name: Battle of Las Queseras del Medio
battles.casualties: About 8 patriots and up to 400 royalists

battles.name: Battle of Vargas Swamp
battles.casualties: Roughly 300–900 dead on both sides

battles.name: Battle of Boyacá
battles.casualties: About 66 patriots and 250 royalists killed or wounded; 1,600 royalists captured

battles.name: Battle of Carabobo
battles.casualties: About 300 patriots and 2,900 royalists killed, wounded or captured

battles.name: Battle of Bomboná
battles.casualties: Heavy losses on both sides; Bolívar's army could not take Pasto

battles.name: Battle of Pichincha
battles.casualties: About 340 patriots and 590 royalists killed or wounded; about 1,260 royalists captured

battles.name: Battle of Junín
battles.casualties: About 150 patriots and 250 royalists killed

battles.name: Battle of Ayacucho
battles.casualties: About 1,000 patriots and 2,500 royalists killed or wounded; 2,000–3,000 royalists captured

battles.name: Siege of Callao
battles.casualties: Defenders: about 780 killed and 1,300 dead of disease; thousands of refugees in the fortress died

battles.name: Battle of Tumusla
battles.casualties: Few; the royalist general Olañeta was mortally wounded
